item.title: The Seahawks are living in the worst of both worlds in the red zone
item.description: Seattle’s red zone offense is bad, and its red zone defense is somehow worse.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks are 4-4, just lost by 17 points to the Chicago Bears on Monday night, yet still have a +26 point differential. Turnovers have obviously been a huge factor in three of their four defeats, but a season-long issue for Seattle’s offense and defense has been seemingly unshakeable.

Neither unit is getting the job done in the red zone.

Seattle’s offense is one of the worst in the red zone

Seattle’s offense ranks a dismal 29th in red zone touchdown percentage, scoring just 13 TDs on 28 trips. If you look at points per red zone trip, which obviously includes field goals, Seattle still ranks 29th. For whatever reason, even though red zone performance is supposedly a high-variance statistic, the Seahawks have not once fielded a top-16 offense in points per red zone possession in the post-Russell Wilson era. This is currently the worst Seahawks offense in the red zone since 2016, when they had a mostly injured Wilson at quarterback, a heavily injured running back unit, and an offensive line that was a total horror show.

While the red zone encompasses the 20-yard line and in, there’s an observation I’ve made throughout the season with Brian Fleury’s playcalling. When the Seahawks are faced with a goal-to-go situation, Fleury’s default move is to run the ball to mixed (at best) results. I’m not joking: 12 runs to 1 pass. The pass was a touchdown to Cooper Kupp in the hurry-up offense against the Washington Commanders, by the way.

No other team (at least using Stathead play-by-play data) is more run-heavy on first-and-goal than Seattle. Only the New York Giants and Cleveland Browns have thrown it once on first-and-goal. Last season, the Seahawks had a pass-run ratio of 14:19 on first-and-goal, and while the red zone offense was also lackluster under Klint Kubiak, they were not extraordinarily predictable.

The first-and-goal runs are not the main reason Seattle is a poor red zone offense, but it’s certainly a factor. We’ve seen very little play-action in the red zone on any down, and the Seahawks roster generally lacks a true “go up and get it” receiving target. That last bit is mostly opinion, but you can probably count the number of high-point catches made by Seahawks receivers on one hand this year—Jaxon Smith-Njigba included. It’s not a strength of this roster and it has to be something Seattle considers when it inevitably examines how to improve the offense next season.

Seattle’s red zone defense is the worst in the NFL

This part is stunning. The Seahawks defense as a whole is still playing very well, but they’re losing in the key situational areas at an alarming rate. They rank 32nd in red zone efficiency, conceding touchdowns on 15 of 18 possessions. Last year they were the fifth-best at preventing red zone touchdowns, and now they’re just bleeding them every trip.

By FTN’s DVOA, they are last in red zone pass, red zone rush, and goal-to-go situations. This probably would matter less if the Seahawks offense wasn’t performing so poorly regardless of where they are on the field, but Seattle is costing themselves wins with these weekly disparities.

And while this is a post about the red zone, the Seahawks defense is the worst 4th down unit in the NFL, giving up 10 of 11 conversions. It’s not the only area where they’ve fallen off.

Seattle became Super Bowl champions last season by “chasing edges” and winning the games within the game. The little things that add up to victories. They’re getting their asses kicked in the margins, and if the red zone performances don’t improve soon, they’ll find themselves missing the playoffs for the fourth time in six seasons.

item.title: Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' QB/TE/DEF/K Blueprint for Week 9
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Hayden Winks lays out the blueprint to the onesies (QB, TE, DEF and K) for Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be an RB column, a WR column and this combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position are available.

Week 9 Projected Points

Week 9 QB Rankings

1. Joe Burrow (at ATL)

Burrow has been dealing as the season-long QB2 (26.2 PPG), generating +0.23 EPA per dropback (QB5). He is lighting up box scores through the air, leading the league in passing yards per game (302) and passing touchdowns per game (2.9). Cincinnati is leaning all the way into his arm, operating with a league-high 66% neutral pass rate (first).

That aggressive approach meets an Atlanta defense allowing 16.3 half PPR points per game to quarterbacks (23rd), where recent signal-callers like Tyler Huntley (24.0 points) and Caleb Williams (16.5 points) have put up functional days. The Bengals head in as 3-point road favorites with an implied team total of 27.25 points (sixth).

2. Josh Allen (at MIN)

Allen's 28.2 fantasy points per game is currently ahead of the all-time fantasy record at QB (Lamar Jackson, 2024). He's done so without DJ Moore for half of the season. Moore was used properly last week with unlimited run-away routes, and then Dalton Kincaid found space downfield in multi-TE sets. It's a great formula.

The Vikings have been by far the best fantasy QB defense, however, allowing just 10.4 fantasy points per game. That's insane. Truly. They haven't faced an elite dual-threat QB this season, though.

Allen will be blitzed at a career-high rate, most likely. He's the QB5 in EPA per dropback against the blitz (+0.07), but that is far lower than on non-blitzes (+0.21, QB1). When blitzed, Allen has a 3.4% scramble rate compared to a 9% scramble rate when not blitzed. It's possible the Bills run a bit more often because of the pressure, as opposing offenses to Minnesota only pass 45% of the time in neutral situations (31st).

Buffalo enters as 3.5-point road favorites carrying an implied team total of 25.0 points (11th). It would make sense for Allen's fantasy output to take a hit here.

3. Brock Purdy (vs. LV)

We'll see if Mike Evans (Achilles) can return, but it doesn't sound like Deebo Samuel Sr. will be back.

Purdy has been surgical as fantasy's QB4 (21.7 PPG), leading all qualified quarterbacks with +0.31 EPA per dropback (QB1). Over his last four starts against quality opponents, his efficiency has cooled to +0.03 EPA per dropback (16th) while averaging 17.3 fantasy points per game. His Week 7 outing without his starting receivers was his worst game of the year (16.0).

He draws a dream matchup against a Raiders defense that's allowing the fourth-most half PPR points per game to QBs (21.8). Las Vegas sits at the top right of the intersection between success rate and explosive rate allowed on dropbacks alongside the worst defenses in the NFL. It's allowed four straight QBs to finish as top-12 QBs. The 49ers enter as 9.5-point home favorites with a slate-leading implied team total of 30.5 points (first).

4. Jared Goff (at MIA)

The Goff outlier dud happened last week, finishing as the QB21 against the Vikings' chaotic defense. Despite that, Goff is the QB4 in EPA per dropback and pacing for 4,770 yards with 36 passing touchdowns. He's the QB6 in fantasy despite not having anything to show with his legs.

The Week 9 environment is pristine against a Miami defense allowing 20.8 half PPR points per game to QBs (sixth). Opposing quarterbacks have moved the ball against the Dolphins regularly, including recent outings from Joe Burrow (24.6 points), Geno Smith (23.5 points) and Drake Maye (22.4 points). Miami is struggling on play action and throws over the middle. That's the entire Lions offense. Detroit is listed as 7-point road favorites with a 28.75-point implied team total (third).

5. Drake Maye (vs. GB)

After a very slow start, Maye is the QB2 from Week 4 on, sandwiched between Joe Burrow and Josh Allen. This past month, his +0.39 EPA per dropback leads the position. He's been the QB14 in EPA per dropback throughout the season, but timely scrambles and plenty of volume have made up for the efficiency decline. We'll see if A.J. Brown and Hunter Henry can suit up later, but Maye made it work with backups against the Dolphins last week (QB7).

He now faces a Packers defense that has kept QBs in check with a chaotic defensive style, surrendering just 14.9 half PPR points per game to the position (27th). Green Bay recently held Bryce Young to 12.4 points, Jared Goff to 18.0 and Dak Prescott to 15.0. The Patriots head into the matchup as 3-point home favorites with an implied team total of 25.25 points (10th).

6. Caleb Williams (vs. TB)

Williams is simply way more accurate this year. He's the QB2 in completion percentage over expected when adjusting for his throw depth. He's middle of the pack in sack rate (7.6%). And he's the QB4 in interception rate. Williams is seeing it extremely well, despite already facing the Vikings, Seahawks, Patriots and the feisty Falcons defenses. He's the QB3 in EPA per dropback, and he'll start spiking fantasy outings once he's pushed by the opponent.

The Bucs defense will be another tough defense to beat. They're fifth-best against fantasy QBs, and from Week 3 on, they've been the best defense in EPA per play, allowing just 15.8 points per game. They slowed down Dak Prescott in Week 5, then completely shut down Bryce Young and Michael Penix Jr. in the past two weeks. They have better pass-rushing depth and have enjoyed full breakouts from CBs Zyon McCollum and especially Jacob Parrish. Tampa Bay also wants to grind out the clock with a run game that is breaking my brain. Chicago returns home as 5.5-point home favorites sporting a 26.5-point implied team total (seventh).

7. Dak Prescott (at IND)

It hasn't been the best Prescott season, and the Cowboys' run game has been so bad that they've lost some inexcusable games along the way. The good news is Prescott has healthy WR and OL units right now, and his defense looks as pathetic as usual. He's been the QB13 in fantasy points per game this year on just QB8 EPA per dropback. It's been much higher than that for long stretches, and I can see that coming back after a recent stretch of games against BAL, HOU, TB and GB. Prescott was the QB6 and QB11 in the last two games against softer opponents.

The Colts defense is one of the worst in the NFL, possibly the worst without DT DeForest Buckner. They were smoked by the Jaguars last week after firing their GM in late October. Dallas heads on the road as 6-point road favorites with a healthy implied team total of 28.5 points (fourth). There are truly no excuses here.

8. Jayden Daniels (vs. LAR)

Jayden Daniels has been the QB15, QB3, QB7 and QB16 in his healthiest games. Since returning from an elbow dislocation, the Commanders have yet to call a designed run for him. He'll still scramble like a madman, but more of those are resulting in slides and running out of bounds early, too. This will hurt him on the margins, though he's still the QB1 in rushing yards per game (47.2).

The Rams present a fun matchup dynamic, ranking 21st in half PPR points allowed to opposing QBs (17.0 per game) but fourth in points allowed specifically to QB rushing. Opposing offenses facing Los Angeles also feature a 47% neutral pass rate, the third-lowest rate allowed in the NFL. Washington hosts this contest as 5.5-point home underdogs carrying a 21.0-point implied team total (23rd).

9. Patrick Mahomes (vs. NYJ)

Mahomes was quite good last week considering the circumstances, finishing as the QB5 against a healthy Broncos defense. Across the year, Mahomes is the QB14 on QB12 EPA per dropback. He was slowed down by the Seahawks without Rashee Rice in Week 7, but the Chiefs have been one of the best offenses in the NFL when not facing a top-three defense this year. Their weaknesses at LT and WR are hidden best against mediocre opponents.

Insert the Jets, who may not have their top-two defensive linemen here. The Jets just allowed top-five fantasy outings from Kirk Cousins, Malik Willis and Drake Maye in their last three outings. It's obviously a great spot here. Kansas City enters as 9.5-point home favorites with a 28.75-point implied team total (third).

Lawrence is up to QB2 overall in EPA per dropback. He hasn't been pushed many times this year, so he's left fourth quarters without adding to his totals. He's only the QB16 in yards per game, leaving him with QB8 fantasy points per game. That's closer to his floor while everyone is healthy on offense. His ceiling is far higher when games are tighter.

That's the issue with the Thursday Night Game against third-string QB Joe Fagnano. The Ravens are 10-point dogs with a team total below 15 points. The Ravens defense is far more talented and far better coached than their current No. 15 ranking in fantasy points allowed to QBs, too. Nice field position and the occasional 1-on-1 loss downfield with Marlon Humphrey in coverage are enough to combat these minor risks for T-Law as a low-end QB1. The Jaguars are ninth in team total (24.75).

11. Jordan Love (at NE)

Love is playing the sport like nobody else. His absurd aggressiveness and arm talent are amazing to watch every week.

Love has turned into the QB9 on a per-game basis, with the second-most yards per game (281). His top three pass catchers are healthy, and they're starting to figure out the best starting OL and ways to hide them on the margins. He's scored multiple touchdowns in 7 of 8 starts. Even with Josh Jacobs in the fold, the Packers have maintained their pass-first identity. That's how it should be behind this OL.

His Week 9 draw is tougher on paper against a New England defense that ranks 22nd in half PPR points allowed to quarterbacks (16.6). The Packers head on the road as 3-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 22.25 points (17th). That's lower than normal.

The Dolphins are definitely better in November than in September. This is the youngest team in the NFL, and it's a new scheme with a new QB. Some of that is because of a Caleb Douglas sideline YAC TD, but him being in the lineup is helpful! Miami is still 30th in neutral pass rate (44%), but they'll be forced to pass here.

The Lions have allowed the most fantasy points to QBs, and opposing offenses have the third-highest neutral pass rate allowed. Their run defense is simply better than their secondary. Detroit will miss star LB Jack Campbell over the middle (and I really hope things progress for him, beyond football), but they did get star S Brian Branch back recently. The Lions have given up the seventh-most rushing QB points this year, partially because of garbage time scrambles. Those count for us! Willis will try to continue this top-12 QB streak, after Kyler Murray (QB10), Jordan Love (QB12), Jacoby Brissett (QB7) and Bryce Young (QB7) have done just that this month. Miami carries a 21.75-point implied team total (18th) as 7-point home underdogs.

I wasn't surprised to see Monday's report that his elbow is sore. That's what his throwing motion looks like right now, and the offense being extremely quick-hitting is further evidence of just that. He now faces a Washington defense allowing the third-most half PPR points per game to quarterbacks (22.0). item.title: Caleb Williams Week 8 QB Grade: Bears @ Seahawks Film Breakdown
item.description: A deeper look with @iamcogs at Caleb Willaims and the Chicago Bears’ blowout 34-17 win against the Seahawks!
item.content:encoded:
Note: Before kicking things off this week, just a quick note. Play breakdowns wont be available this week due to traveling for work, these will continue for week 9. In their stead I added some more interesting data points and nuggets to fill out this weeks’ breakdown.

If last week was about Caleb Williams showing he could attack a defense in just about any way it presented itself, Week 8 was about proving he could do it against one of the best units in football.

Seattle entered Monday night with the NFL’s No. 1 defense, allowing just 144.4 passing yards per game. No quarterback had reached 200 yards against them all season, and the Seahawks hadn’t allowed more than 301 total yards in any of their first seven games. Justin Herbert couldn’t do it. Brock Purdy couldn’t do it. Patrick Mahomes couldn’t do it.

Williams did.

On the road. In primetime. At Lumen Field. Against the defending Super Bowl champions.

If we’re weighing opponent, environment and situation, this might have been the most impressive performance Williams has put on tape this season.

He completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions, finishing with a 101.0 passer rating as Chicago walked out of Seattle with a 34-17 win. Williams became the first quarterback to crack 200 passing yards against the Seahawks this season, while the Bears finished with 363 total yards against a defense that had entered the week allowing fewer than 302 in every game.

The tone was set immediately.

After Chicago’s defense opened the game with a three-and-out, Williams took the offense on a 17-play, 80-yard touchdown drive that burned 8:32 off the clock. He completed eight of 10 passes on the possession before extending a second down play and finding Luther Burden III for the opening score.

Seattle hadn’t allowed an opening-drive touchdown in 16 games, and opponents had gone 17 consecutive possessions without even reaching the Seahawks’ red zone.

Chicago broke both streaks on its first opportunity, and like they have done so much this season already, never looked back.

That opening possession ended up being a pretty good preview of how the rest of the night would go. The Bears weren’t necessarily explosive on every drive, but they remained patient, stayed on schedule and made Seattle’s defense work for everything. Chicago finished with 70 offensive plays and held the football for 35:03, continuing a season-long trend of controlling games through sustained possessions. Bill Zimmerman highlighted just how dominant that time-of-possession battle has become over the season.

The broader offensive results when Williams has been able to play a full game have been just as encouraging, which is becoming harder to dismiss as a small-sample fluke with each passing week.

And this wasn’t a Seattle defense suddenly playing poorly before Chicago arrived.

According to SumerSports, Seattle had not allowed positive offensive EPA in a single game all season. The Bears became just the fourth team since the start of 2025 to generate positive EPA against Mike Macdonald’s defense.

That’s important context when looking at Williams’ raw stat line.

247 yards and one touchdown probably isn’t going to jump off the page after back-to-back 300-yard games, but this was never going to be the type of matchup where the numbers told the entire story. Seattle’s defense is designed to affect the quarterback with four rushers, keep bodies in coverage and force an offense to string together long possessions without making mistakes.

Williams largely did exactly that.

He continued to play efficient football even in obvious passing situations, something George Hatzadony’s charting has consistently highlighted this season, while also showing the same ability to create when Seattle disrupted the pocket.

That second part continues to be one of the more encouraging developments of his season.

Williams has always had the physical ability to escape pressure. The difference now is that more of those plays are ending with productive decisions rather than simply becoming extended chaos or balls that end up thrown away. PFN noted this week that Williams is one of only four qualifying quarterbacks producing positive EPA under pressure this season, joining Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes and Drake Maye.

There were several examples Monday night where Williams escaped the initial rush, reset and still delivered an accurate football rather than immediately abandoning the structure of the play.

That balance has become increasingly noticeable. The highlight-reel improvisation is still there, but it isn’t replacing the offense anymore. It’s supplementing it.

You could see that especially when Williams began attacking Rome Odunze after halftime. Odunze finished with four catches for 87 yards, with gains of 23 and 22 yards helping set up Chicago’s third-quarter touchdown. Williams consistently attacked the intermediate areas of Seattle’s coverage, an area where the Seahawks had been one of the league’s better defenses entering the game.

And when Seattle finally made its push in the fourth quarter, Chicago answered.

A Colston Loveland fumble gave the Seahawks a short field and allowed them to cut the lead to 20-17. Lumen Field suddenly sounded like Lumen Field again, and for the first time all night it felt like momentum had completely shifted.

The Bears responded with a six-play, 56-yard touchdown drive.

The biggest play came on third-and-9 when Williams got the football quickly to Kalif Raymond, who split the defense for 39 yards on what was officially a run play. D’Andre Swift finished the drive with his second touchdown.

That’s another area where this team continues to look different.

Chicago isn’t simply surviving close games anymore. When opponents have made their push, the Bears have increasingly answered by taking control right back.

The 17-point victory was Seattle’s first loss by more than four points in 30 games, including the postseason. Their previous six losses dating back to the start of the 2025 season had come by 17 combined points.

Chicago beat them by 17 in one night.

Williams also quietly added another piece of NFL history. Monday marked his 36th consecutive regular-season game with at least 20 pass attempts and no more than one interception, breaking Aaron Rodgers’ previous record of 35.

He also became the first quarterback in Bears history to lead the offense to 30-plus points in three consecutive games without committing a turnover, another sign of how consistently clean his football has become.

Tom Brady even called Williams the “perfect quarterback” for Ben Johnson’s offense, praising the way Johnson uses Williams’ skill set within an offense that can attack defenses through the run game, quick passing, explosives, screens and misdirection.

That’s really what the last three weeks have shown.

Atlanta tried to keep everything underneath, so Williams patiently took the completions.

New England brought pressure and gave him opportunities downfield, so he punished them with eight explosive completions.

Seattle brought the league’s best defense into one of the toughest environments in football and dared Chicago to methodically work its way down the field.

Williams did that too.

The Bears have now scored at least 30 points in three straight games since his return, and they haven’t trailed for a single second during that stretch.

Oh, and Chicago just became the first team in NFL history to beat both participants from the previous Super Bowl in back-to-back primetime games.

Patriots on Thursday night.

Defending champion Seahawks in Seattle on Monday night.

Two wins.

If you wanted a stretch that starts making people view this team a little differently, that’s probably it.

Now let’s get into the numbers.

Benchmarks

(Season totals are underlined, Season Averages in Italics, and this week’s stats appear in regular text.)

C/A:88/124 (71.0%) | 22/31 (71.0%) | 24/34 70.6%

Yards:1020 | 255 | 247

Touchdowns:6 | 1.5 | 1

Turnovers: 1| 0.3 | 0

QB at Fault Sacks:1 |0.3| 0

aDOT:6.6 | 9.4

Passer Rating: 105.6 | 101.0

True Passer Rating:119.1 | 139.7

Time to Throw:3.23s | 2.87s

Time to Pressure:2.55s | 2.54s

Pressure Rate:38.87% | 27.78%

On-Target Rate:88.0% | 78.1%

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 3.5% PPR /7.6% BRP | 0.0% PPR /10.8% BRP

EPA per dropback:+0.28 | +0.40

ANY/A: 7.3 | 9.1

Game Scorecard

The full grading sheet for each play can be found here.

Game Notes

Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score, which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward.

NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 101.0 / 139.7 / 78.0

  • The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 8 sits at 91.5, putting Williams’ 101.0 against Seattle comfortably above average.
    • Four of Williams’ five starts have now produced a passer rating north of 100. He reached that mark just five times across the entire 2025 season, another one of the many markers of growth we’ve seen so far.
  • A 139.7 TPR represents a great outing, built once again around measured aggression without putting the football in harm’s way.
    • Williams’ 9.4 aDOT was his highest since Week 1, which makes the performance even more impressive considering the quality of the defense he was facing.
  • On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Williams finished Week 8 with a 78.0 Impact Score, ranking 10th among qualifying quarterbacks.

On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 84.9% | Week 8: 78.1%

  • Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target.
  • Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 18/20 | 90.0% On-Target
  • Deep-Level Passing (10+ Yards Downfield): 7/12 | 58.3% On-Target
    • Williams remained deadly accurate underneath, missing on just two short-level throws all night.
    • There were a few misses farther downfield that I’m not particularly concerned about. One deep shot to Rome Odunze late in the first half came with the pocket collapsing, while another pressure-affected throw sailed harmlessly out of bounds. The high miss to Zavion Thomas was more notable for a few reasons, and we’ll break that one down later.

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 0.0% PPR / 10.8% BPR

  • Williams now sits at roughly a 2.9% Poor Play Rate and 8.2% Big Play Rate on the season.
    • What might be the most impressive part of his Seattle performance is that Williams didn’t record a single “Poor” or turnover-worthy play against one of the league’s best defenses.
    • At the same time, he posted a 10.8% Big Play Rate with three “Great” plays and one “Elite.”
      • The “Great” throws included a beautifully layered ball over the middle to Luther Burden III, the 23-yard dig to Rome Odunze following the direct snap to D’Andre Swift, and another anticipatory dig to Odunze for an explosive gain.
      • His lone “Elite” play came after escaping what looked like a sure sack, regaining his composure and firing a dart downfield to Odunze for another 22 yards.

EPA per Dropback: 2026 Average: +0.28 | Week 8: +0.14

  • Williams’ +0.14 EPA/dropback was about half his season average, but the opponent matters quite a bit here. Seattle entered Week 8 having not allowed positive offensive EPA in a single game all season.
    • A fun little nugget within the larger EPA conversation: Williams has been lethal on third down this season, leading the league in third-down EPA according to this charting.
    • EPA isn’t everything, but continuing to produce positive efficiency against a defense that had largely erased opposing offenses all season is another point in Williams’ favor.

ANY/A: 2026 Average: 7.3 | Week 8: 7.3

  • Williams landed directly on his season average with a 7.3 ANY/A against Seattle. The 2026 league average currently sits at 6.2.
    • Doing that against this particular defense adds some important context. Seattle entered Week 8 allowing just 3.5 ANY/A to opposing passers.
    • Williams more than doubled that number, on the road, in one of the league’s toughest environments. That’s an exceptional performance relative to the matchup.

Time to Throw: 2026 Average: 3.16s | Week 8: 2.87s

  • For the first time this season, Williams finished under three seconds in my Time to Throw charting, averaging 2.87 seconds across 36 dropbacks.
    • When Chicago wasn’t looking to exploit a matchup downfield, the offense was content to use quick-hitting routes underneath to neutralize Seattle’s front four.
    • It worked. Williams was sacked just once, while my charting had Seattle generating pressure on a season-low 27.78% of his dropbacks.

Hurry Up!

  • One of my favorite follows on Twitter breaks this down better than I ever could, but Chicago shifted into hurry-up twice in goal-to-go situations to prevent Seattle from substituting and force the defense to remain in favorable personnel.
    • Both situations came from essentially the same formation, with Ben Johnson adding a different wrinkle the second time around.
    • It’s another example of the extra layer Johnson brings to the offense, but just as importantly, it shows how comfortable this group has become executing those adjustments on the fly.

Summary

Williams finishes Week 8 with final grades of 1st Half (2.85) / 2nd Half (2.25) / Game (5.10), with the snap threshold adjustment bumping his final score to 5.30. This scores solidly as a “Good” outing, his fourth in five starts.

It doesn’t quite reach the 6.30 grades he posted against Carolina and New England, but considering the circumstances, I think there’s a strong argument this was his most impressive performance of the season.

Seattle entered Monday night with the best defense in football, hadn’t allowed a 200-yard passer all season and had consistently made life miserable for opposing quarterbacks. Williams walked into one of the league’s toughest environments in primetime, against the defending Super Bowl champions, and never really looked overwhelmed by any of it. He didn’t have to play superhero ball either. Chicago stayed patient, kept the offense on schedule and consistently found answers when Seattle tried to change the picture.

That’s reflected in the grading as much as anything else. Williams didn’t register a single “Poor” or turnover-worthy play while still producing four “Great” or “Elite” plays. He finished with a 10.8% Big Play Rate, pushed his aDOT back up to 9.4 yards and still managed to play clean football against a defense that had entered the week suffocating opposing passing games.

The stat line probably won’t be remembered the same way as the back-to-back 300-yard performances that preceded it, but I don’t think it needs to be. This was another example of Williams showing he can win in a different way depending on what the defense demands from him. His ability to keep the offense on schedule cannot be overstated, the Bears averaged just 3.6 yards per rush, while D’Andre Swift averaged 2.6, but Caleb’s ability to move the ball allowed Swift 3 rushing touchdowns, putting him in the league lead with 10 on the year.

Of the six quarterbacks I’m grading this season, Williams finished 1st of the five who played in Week 8. You can see where his performance landed among the group here.

For a look at how the entire group stacks up on the season, along with some quick notes on this week’s performances, you can find that here.

The Bears now return home at 6-2 for another primetime matchup, this time against Tampa Bay on Sunday Night Football. The Buccaneers may only be 3-5, but they’re suddenly playing considerably better football after consecutive wins over Carolina and Atlanta. Tampa just shut out the Falcons 16-0 while running for a franchise-record 324 yards, so this isn’t exactly a matchup Chicago can sleepwalk through.

Three straight wins since his return, three straight games with at least 30 points and another strong grade against the best defense he’s faced all season.

Not a bad way to keep this thing rolling.

Until next time, Bear Down!

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

It is course-correction time in the NFL.

Tuesday’s trade deadline looms large, and with teams headed in different directions as the season wears on, NFL insiders believe this year’s list of deals could be larger than ever. One team, the Indianapolis Colts, has already shifted into seller mode and another, the Chicago Bears, swung for the fences in a deal for defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons.

What other trades could be around the corner?

Let’s dive into the latest rumors.

Colts now waiting to see

When the Indianapolis Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard, it sparked the first run of trades from an organization that looks to be starting a rebuild. The Colts traded guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks, and sent DeForest Buckner back to the NFC West in a deal with the San Francisco 49ers.

Those moves, coupled with wide receiver Josh Downs asking for a trade himself, sparked the idea of a “fire sale” in Indianapolis. Not only could Downs help an offense that is hoping for a deep playoff run, but running back Jonathan Taylor might be the most intriguing player potentially available ahead of Tuesday’s deadline.

But Indianapolis might be hitting the pause button on that fire sale, at least for a few days. According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Colts are waiting to see how Week 9’s game against the Dallas Cowboys goes before “revisiting the offers on the table and making the trades that make sense on Monday and Tuesday ahead of the deadline:”

Here at SB Nation, we looked at potential landing spots for both Taylor and Downs already.

Those teams might have to wait a few more days before a trade can be finalized.

What about the Cowboys?

What about those Dallas Cowboys?

Dallas is in a fascinating position. The Cowboys are sitting at 3-5 and coming off a brutal overtime loss to the Arizona Cardinals, which might lead you to believe they will be sellers at the deadline. But that same 3-5 record is good enough for second in the NFC East, and just one game behind the New York Giants in the win column.

So what will the Cowboys do?

One thing they will not do, reportedly, is trade wide receiver George Pickens. NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported he would be “beyond stunned” if the team moved the wide receiver:

While Pickens is not under contract for next year, Rapoport notes that between the NFC East, and the easy schedule coming up, he has a hard time believing that the Cowboys would be sellers at the deadline.

But could they actually be buyers?

Over at ESPN, Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano believe that the Cowboys could make yet another addition to a defense that continues to struggle, identifying Arizona pass rusher Josh Sweat as an option.

Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat has been linked to Dallas, which could be in the pass rush market but hasn’t made any moves there yet. The sense I get from teams in the edge rusher market is that Sweat would prefer a new deal as part of a trade — or at least a sweetener, such as a raise on his $18.1 million salary this year or next. He’s in the second year of a four-year, $76 million contract, so wanting it reworked so early in the deal could be a hurdle to a trade.

After adding so many pieces to the defense over the past year, through free agency, trades, and the draft, Jerry Jones could be motivated to add one more.

Bears not done?

The Chicago Bears already made a big addition to the defensive line, bringing in Jeffery Simmons in a deal with the Tennessee Titans. That trade paid immediate dividends in Chicago’s Week 8 win over the Seattle Seahawks. Consider these statistics from Bears beat writer Courtney Cronin:

According to Next Gen Stats, the Seahawks were held to 3.0 yards per play (3 sacks, INT) in the 48 plays where Simmons was on the field. In the eight plays where he was off the field, Seattle averaged 13.3 yards per play.

Darnold completed less than 50% of his passes with Simmons on the field and was a perfect 5-of-5 with a touchdown when he was off.

But could Chicago add another player to that defensive front?

Seth Walder believes they could, and is looking at Miami Dolphins pass rusher Josh Uche as that player:

“Dolphins edge Josh Uche,” Walder wrote. “The Bears already paid a ton to bring in Simmons, so I assume they’ll be seeking bargains for the rest of deadline season. But they still could use some help at edge, and Uche could contribute to that rotation alongside Montez Sweat, Austin Booker and Daniel Hardy. This season, Uche has recorded a pass rush win rate that ranks in the 60th percentile and a pressure rate in the 35th percentile at edge.”

Adding Uche on the edge would give that defensive line another big boost.

Steelers not trading for a WR?

A consistent rumor this fall has held that the Pittsburgh Steelers would be adding a wide reciever, to give Aaron Rodgers another target in the passing game as the team looks towards a playoff push.

But longtime Pittsburgh insider Gerry Dulac poured some cold water on that idea Wednesday.

In his weekly chat with readers, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette scribe was asked several questions about the Steelers adding a WR ahead of the deadline. Dulac pushed back on those rumors each time.

“They’re not seriously pursuing any,” Dulac wrote. “What I’m hearing is they are not likely or intending to make a trade, but as I always say, never under-estimate the desperation of an NFL GM who might coming knocking for a deal.”

Pittsburgh has made additions to the WR room over the past two years. The Steelers traded for DK Metcalf ahead of the 2025 season, traded for Michael Pittman Jr. this past offseason, and drafted both Germie Bernard and Kaden Wetjen this past spring. While Steelers fans might love the idea of one more WR, they might be disappointed come Tuesday night.

What about Brian Thomas Jr.?

Astute observers noted something when the Jacksonville Jaguars posted a Halloween message that read in part “Weapons,” featuring some of the talented players around quarterback Trevor Lawrence.

Specifically, they noted the lack of Brian Thomas Jr.:

A first-round pick in 2024, Thomas has never quite lived up to the billing in Jacksonville. And teams that need WR help should at least be inquiring about his availablity.

Two such teams? The Kansas City Chiefs and the San Francisco 49ers. Both teams have endured injuries at the WR spot, and both teams should be looking at adding to that position ahead of the deadline.

item.content:encoded:

While the expectation is that they will get several players back from injured reserve at some point, they also could go for a more radical approach in hopes of improving their team and gearing up for a stretch run in 2026. item.title: Fantasy Football Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Joel Smyth offers FLEX lineup advice for Quinshon Judkins, Raiders RBs, more players in Week 9
item.description: Joel Smyth helps you through those tough flex decisions for your Week 9 fantasy football lineups.
item.content:encoded:
We're on to Week 9 of the fantasy football season! As we look for every advantage this season, the X-factor position is the FLEX. To break it all down, Yahoo analyst Joel Smyth goes through 8 players in the consensus rankings flex zone for your flexes, double flexes or even third WR slots.

​Set & Forget

Jonah Coleman, RB, DEN vs. CAR

It's time. Jonah Coleman completely took over the backfield in Week 8, handling 11 of 13 carries after J.K. Dobbins opened with the first five. He had five targets, six opportunities at the goal line and a big fantasy day versus a top RB defense. The Panthers, on the other end, just fired their defensive coordinator. Denver, despite a slow start, ranks 10th in RB fantasy points in the first half of the season. With no RJ Harvey, plenty of valuable touches are available to the rookie in a great situation as a whole. Coleman has been the far more successful back and should be treated like such this weekend.

Jameson Williams, WR, DET vs. MIA

Miami is a top-five matchup against wide receivers this season and its passing defense has been terrible. On a per-play basis, the Dolphins rank dead last; they just have not been thrown on much this season. Williams isn't volume-dependent, and he may need to hit early on versus the Dolphins to hit at all, but Miami's improvement on offense, paired with the Lions defense, can help.

Over the last month, Miami ranks 14th in scoring offense, which hopefully can keep it close to the powerhouse that is Detroit's offense, entering as touchdown underdogs. Williams' targets aren't always consistent or high, but they have been valuable downfield shots and in the red zone in a top offense, making the overall volume much closer to that of a fantasy WR2 over the last month. He's become a weekly set-and-forget with his production as of late.

Flex Starts

Quinshon Judkins, RB, CLE vs. NO

With Dylan Sampson back, Judkins becomes much more game-script dependent. That game script has a better shot of staying in his favor this week as 2.5-point underdogs to New Orleans, hopefully a closer game than the 21-point loss to Pittsburgh last weekend. In the Browns' five wins this season, Judkins has scored 14.4 half-PPR PPG, handling an extreme share of the backfield carries and all the goal-line work. The Saints have been an RB's dream so far in 2026, ranking 32nd versus backs on the season, only getting worse over the last five games.​

Ashton Jeanty, RB, LV vs. SF

The Jeanty experience has not been for the faint of heart. What we don't know is how this backfield will be split on the ground this week — the Raiders potentially sticking with Mike Washington Jr. completely, going back to 50-50 or (unlikely) swinging all the way back to Jeanty as the workhorse. What we do know is that there is a 90% chance Jeanty is the receiving back, something that alone would make him the RB22 in PPR scoring, as he's scored the most receiving fantasy points at the position.

We also know that, although the 49ers have been the best defense in the NFL versus rushing fantasy points, they also rank 32nd against RB receiving points. I'm not confident if he's my RB1 or RB2, but I still believe Jeanty is worthy of a flex spot.​

Double Flex Only

Rome Odunze, WR, CHI vs TB

Maybe give one more week for Odunze. This week I had a personal favorite come out with the Heaven versus Hell Graph, comparing the first half of the season schedule to the second half. Odunze is where you'd want him with a much better schedule going forward … after this week. From Weeks 10-17, there isn't a spot you're scared of, but Week 9's matchup versus Tampa Bay isn't ideal.

Odunze will match up against Zyon McCollum on nearly half of the plays this Sunday. McCollum is allowing a very low amount of production when targeted against, to begin with. The Bucs' defense had been dominant against the pass long before Week 8 versus Atlanta, ranking No. 1 (over Minnesota!) in EPA/pass on the season.

Kyle Pitts Sr., TE, ATL vs. CIN

It's been a rollercoaster for Pitts managers; what's new? This week, hopefully it's a game where you don't regret putting him in your lineup the next morning. There are a couple of main reasons why I think Pitts can be used as the extra flex. No. 1, the Bengals. They were horrible against tight ends last year and are only a little better this season, giving up, on average, 5.3 PPG more than the average defense does to the position. They struggle up the middle in general and often find themselves in shootouts.

No. 2 is that Cincinnati plays a high amount of man coverage. Pitts is the seventh-best in fantasy points per route this season if he were a WR. For the second straight season, QB Michael Penix Jr. and Pitts have been best buds against man coverage, being the primary reason for most big Pitts days. You won't even need coffee Sunday morning for this game abroad if your heart is already racing with Pitts in the starting lineup.

Booby Traps​

Mike Washington Jr., RB, LV vs. SF

The stat breaking down the 49ers' running back defense is why Washington is in the booby traps. San Francisco is 32nd versus receiving backs, but first against rushing, where Washington has an extremely low percentage (10.8%) of his fantasy points from. If Washington does get the volume again, well, there's a good chance it doesn't work out anyway. The Raiders have converted two of their 17 goal-line carries, which is likely what it would take to overcome the 49ers' rushing defense. The floor is very low for multiple reasons, making it a pass for me until we have more knowledge of the split or at least a better matchup.

Zach Charbonnet, RB, SEA vs. ARI

Arizona has shockingly not been a positive matchup for running backs this season. The defense is getting scored on more than any team in the NFL, yet they are second-best against RB fantasy points adjusted to the schedule. Charbonnet is coming off of a major injury with multiple other RB options available.

In Week 8, he only played 20 of 57 snaps on offense. It's not enough for me to trust, with around 10 touches being the expected volume. In the past, spots such as these could be salvaged with the goal-line touchdown, which certainly can happen, but a lower shot with the red-zone work being split three ways last week. It's not a guarantee the goal-line carry goes to Charbonnet if there is one at all.

item.title: Could the 49ers make a deal with the Texans again for a defensive lineman?
item.description: The Texans have a pass rusher who is available and should come cheap in a trade.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers and the Houston Texans have been involved in some business over the past few years.

Back in 2024, the 49ers dealt a seventh-round pick for defensive tackle Maliek Collins in a move that worked out for them for a year. Collins was a solid pass-rusher and went on to sign with the Cleveland Browns, where he’s found even more success, recently signing an extension.

They’ve also traded seventh-round picks to the Texans for defensive tackle Khalil Davis and offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson in separate trades. Now, could it be time for a fourth deal over the past two years?

Heading into the trade deadline, the 49ers already made a splash move, landing DeForest Buckner for a 2027 fourth-round pick to slot in as their new starting defensive tackle. Following that, the 49ers are still actively looking for a pass rusher and a wide receiver, and one of those needs could be filled with a minor trade with the Texans.

CBS Sports mocked a trade between the 49ers and Texans for veteran edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney, with the two sides swapping sixth and seventh-round picks in the deal.

“The Niners have already given their defensive line a boost by trading for DeForest Buckner, and they should welcome Nick Bosa back into the fold soon, if not this week coming off their bye,” CBS Sports’s Jared Dubin wrote. “But they’re still just 21st in the NFL in pressure rate, according to Tru Media, and they have been dealing with injuries along the defensive front all season. Adding another capable rotational player off the edge could give them an extra boost ahead of a potential playoff run.”

In the deal, the 49ers are receiving a 2027 seventh-round pick, while sending out a 2028 sixth-round pick.

Clowney has been a name that has popped up in trade conversations this week, as he’s played under 40 percent of the defensive snaps for the Texans and is 33 years old. The 49ers currently have a draft pick in every round but the fourth in the 2027 NFL Draft after the Buckner trade, so they could swap sixths and sevenths this year.

But if they’re asked to move a 2028 pick and get a 2027 in return, the deal could make even more sense. And it could make sense for Houston as well, as they currently don’t have a 2028 sixth-round pick.

If the 49ers are to look for a pass rusher and a wide receiver, at least one of those moves will have to be cheap. San Francisco doesn’t have any projected compensatory picks coming their way this offseason. So two trades could mean two additional picks from their 2027 war chest gone, leaving them with just four draft picks in the class.

A move like this would fill a need while being relatively cheap and adding more leadership to the room with a veteran player who has played in a similar system. Clowney hasn’t been anything special this year, accumulating just nine pressures on 78 pass-rushing snaps. But he’s cheap and a veteran body who can add to a rotation currently ranking 21st in the NFL in pressure rate.

That would also allow the 49ers to look for a receiver and still come out fine on the draft capital side going into the offseason.
